claims.text: The starting material is an equimolar or nearly equimolar, single-phase solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
Adding Ti to CoCrFeNi reduces local chemical order.
Adding Ti to CoCrFeNi lowers the stacking-fault energy.
Local chemical order can alter the energy landscape and activation barriers experienced by moving dislocations in concentrated solid solutions.
Reduced local chemical order decreases the activation barriers for dislocation nucleation and motion in CoCrFeNiTi.
Lower stacking-fault energy facilitates dislocation nucleation and glide in CoCrFeNiTi.
Easier dislocation glide reduces dislocation pile-up in CoCrFeNiTi.
Ti-induced changes cause an earlier onset of dynamic recovery.
Easier dislocation motion, fewer pile-ups, and enhanced dynamic recovery produce lower hardness and yield strength.
CoCrFeNiTi has good plasticity despite its lower hardness and strength.
CoCrFeNiTi has good machinability despite its lower hardness and strength.
Differing levels of local chemical order can produce differing strength, strain-hardening, and ductility at the same overall alloy composition.
Equimolar CoCrFeNi without Ti has a higher density of dislocation obstacles because its local chemical order is not modified by Ti.
Relative to equimolar CoCrFeNi, equimolar CoCrFeNiTi will exhibit lower hardness.
Relative to equimolar CoCrFeNi, equimolar CoCrFeNiTi will exhibit lower yield strength.
Relative to equimolar CoCrFeNi, equimolar CoCrFeNiTi will show more facile dislocation motion and a lower dislocation pile-up density in TEM.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to single-phase, equimolar or nearly equimolar solid solutions under room-temperature mechanical loading at engineering strain rates.
CoCrFeNiTi and CoCrFeNi should be compared using identical processing histories and mechanical-test conditions, with alloy chemistry as the intended variable.
Failure to observe reduced hardness and yield strength, easier glide, or reduced pile-ups in CoCrFeNiTi relative to CoCrFeNi would falsify the hypothesis.
